newsitem.title: USA: Cloudy skies may delay U.S. Mir astronaut's return.
newsitem.headline: Cloudy skies may delay U.S. Mir astronaut's return.

text.p: Bad weather in Florida on Wednesday threatened to delay the landing of the space shuttle Atlantis, which was to bring home U.S. astronaut John Blaha from the Russian Mir space station.
Atlantis was scheduled to touchdown at the Kennedy Space Centre around 7:47 a.m. EST (1247 GMT), but cloudy skies were a problem, NASA officials said.
"The weather forecast is a bit dynamic at the Cape," mission control spokesman Rob Navias said. "It will pose a challenge for flight controllers."
NASA's chief astronaut, Bob Cabana, flying a training jet, reported low level clouds over the shuttle's three mile- (5 km) long landing strip. There was also a chance of patchy ground fog.
Forecasters believed that the bands of cloud would move to the north of the space centre in time for Atlantis' landing.
"Hopefully we'll get you down today sometime," mission control's Kevin Kregel radioed the astronauts.

A second landing opportunity in Florida was available at 9:23 a.m. EST (1423 GMT). Controllers in Houston said they were not considering a landing at the backup runway in California. The astronauts had enough supplies to remain in orbit until Friday if necessary.
The shuttle's 60-ft (18-meters) long clam-like payload bay doors were swung shut at about 4 a.m. EST (0900 GMT) in preparation for the planned landing.

Atlantis was to bring home John Blaha, who spent four months aboard Russia's Mir space station. The 54-year-old astronaut was to ride back to Earth in a reclining chair, his body wired with sensors so doctors could monitor his health as he felt the pull of gravity for the first time in 128 days.

Atlantis docked with Mir last week to collect Blaha and drop off his replacement, Jerry Linenger. The shuttle also delivered more than three tons of supplies and equipment to the 11-year-old space station.
